cap: A synthetase assigns the amino acid to an adaptor; a ribosome selects the adaptor through codon recognition.
Schematic of the Chapeville experiment: chemical conversion changes the attached amino acid without intentionally changing adaptor identity.
Simplified cloverleaf with acceptor stem, D arm, anticodon arm, T arm, variable region and 3′ CCA end; the mature 3-D fold separates the anticodon and aminoacyl termini.
The G3·U70 pair is a major determinant in bacterial alanine tRNA. Replacing the pair can reduce charging; transfer into a suitable scaffold can confer alanine acceptance.
The amino acid carboxylate participates in adenylate formation; PPi is released and can subsequently be hydrolyzed.

t: Acyl transfer to the terminal ribose
cap: The aminoacyl adenylate transfers its acyl group to the terminal ribose, liberating AMP; the amino group remains available.
After noncognate activation, hydrolysis before esterification removes an incorrect adenylate. The lower branch shows the productive transfer route.
Hydrolysis of the ester regenerates intact, uncharged RNA and the free amino acid.
Ile and Val may enter the synthetic pathway. The editing site preferentially removes incorrect Val while retaining the useful Ile product.

t: Distinct sources of a valine substitution
cap: Either a mischarged Ile adaptor or a wrongly selected Val adaptor may cause a Val residue at an Ile codon. The two pathways require different assays.
Initial slopes for wild type and mutant are 0.020 and 0.004 micromolar per second; the values are hypothetical and apply only over the indicated interval.
A deliberately deacylated control identifies the uncharged band. The illustrated bands are schematic; migration order is not a universal property.
The simplified first-order model describes opposing fluxes between charged and uncharged tRNA, with a fixed total pool.
In some organisms a nondiscriminating GluRS charges tRNA for glutamine with glutamate, and amidotransferase converts the attached cargo.
